title: Tomorrow and the weather
goal: Talk about the future in both available ways, discuss the weather, and make plans together.
bekal: using *będę* + dictionary form for activities that will be ongoing
using the completed form for results you'll achieve
talking about weather and seasons, and making conditional plans

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Plan na weekend
dialogs.intro: Thursday afternoon, the campus canteen. Ania opens the weather forecast on her phone.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: What are you doing this weekend?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeszcze nie wiem. Jaka będzie pogoda?
lines.id: I don't know yet. What's the weather going to be like?
lines.literal: still not I-know. what-kind will-be weather?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: W sobotę ma być słonecznie, ale w niedzielę będzie padać.
lines.id: Saturday's supposed to be sunny, but on Sunday it'll rain.
lines.literal: in Saturday has be sunny, but in Sunday will fall.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: To może pojedziemy w sobotę w góry?
lines.id: So how about going to the mountains on Saturday?
lines.literal: so maybe we-will-ride in Saturday to mountains?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Świetny pomysł! Wstaniemy wcześnie i weźmiemy pociąg o siódmej.
lines.id: Great idea! We'll get up early and take the seven o'clock train.
lines.literal: great idea! we-will-get-up early and we-will-take train at seventh.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: W górach zawsze jest chłodniej. Weź kurtkę i czapkę.
lines.id: It's always cooler in the mountains. Take a jacket and a hat.
lines.literal: in mountains always is cooler. take jacket and hat.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dobrze. A co zrobimy, jeśli będzie padać?
lines.id: OK. And what will we do if it rains?
lines.literal: good. and what we-will-do, if will fall?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Wtedy zostaniemy w mieście i pójdziemy do muzeum.
lines.id: Then we'll stay in town and go to a museum.
lines.literal: then we-will-stay in city and we-will-go to museum.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Also good. I'll buy the tickets this evening.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Świetnie. Ja napiszę do reszty grupy.
lines.id: Great. I'll message the rest of the group.
lines.literal: great. I will-write to rest of-group.

notes: **Two ways to talk about the future, and you already have both.** First: *będę* + dictionary form — for activities that will be **ongoing** (*będę czytać* — I'll be reading). Second: the **completed** form with present-tense endings — for results you'll **achieve** (*przeczytam* — I'll finish reading it).

**Pojedziemy, wstaniemy, weźmiemy, kupię, napiszę** — all completed forms, and all of them mean the future. Notice that this dialogue hardly uses *będę* at all: in everyday conversation Poles use the completed form far more often for clear plans.

**Będzie padać** — "it's going to rain". *Padać* literally means "to fall", and in Polish rain really does "fall": *pada deszcz* (rain is falling), *pada śnieg* (snow is falling). Often shortened to just *pada*.
**Ma być słonecznie** — "it's supposed to be sunny". The formula *ma być* is used for forecasts and news that aren't certain yet, just like English "supposed to be".
**W góry** (to the mountains) but **w górach** (in the mountains). Destinations take the object form, locations take *miejscownik* — the unit 14 rule at work again.

**Weź kurtkę** — the command form of *wziąć*. Command forms belong to A2, but a few you'll hear all the time are worth recognizing now: *weź* (take), *chodź* (come on), *powiedz* (tell me), *poczekaj* (wait).
**Jeśli będzie padać** — "if it rains". Notice that Polish uses the **future** in the if-clause, while English uses the present. It's actually more logical, and easy to get used to.
**Nie mogę się doczekać** — "I can't wait". A fixed expression; don't take it apart word by word.

grammars.title: Future, way one: będę + dictionary form
body: Used with **ongoing** verbs, for activities that will be in progress or repeated.
after: There's a second, equally correct version: *będę czytał* (m) / *będę czytała* (f) — using the past form instead of the dictionary form. Poles use both every day; the dictionary-form version is easier for beginners because you don't have to choose a gender.
*Będę* is also used alone to mean "will be (somewhere)": *Będę w domu o szóstej.* — I'll be home at six.
⚠️ *Będę* **can't** be combined with a completed form. *Będę napisać* is wrong; just *napiszę* is right.

grammars.title: Future, way two: the completed form
body: No helper word at all — present-tense endings on a completed verb automatically mean the future.
after: You choose between the two just as in unit 18: if the **result** matters, use the completed form; if the **activity** matters, use *będę*.
Compare: *Jutro będę pisać* (tomorrow I'll be writing, all day long) with *Jutro napiszę* (tomorrow I'll get it written).
For near, fixed plans Polish often just uses the **present tense**, like English "I'm going": *Jutro idę do kina.* — I'm going to the cinema tomorrow.

blocks.title: What surprises newcomers from warmer countries
items: **Day length changes dramatically.** In June the sun sets at almost 9:00 p.m.; in December at 3:30 p.m. This changes how a day feels far more than the temperature does.
**Minus ten isn't as bad as it sounds** — if the wind is calm and you dress in layers. The really miserable month is November: zero degrees, wet and windy.
*Zimno mi.* (I'm cold) and *gorąco mi.* (I'm hot) — two sentences you'll use a lot. Note the form: literally "cold to me".

blocks.title: Linking conditions
items: *Jeśli będzie ładnie, pójdziemy do parku.* — If the weather's nice, we'll go to the park.
*Jeśli będzie padać, zostaniemy w domu.* — If it rains, we'll stay home.
*Kiedy skończę pracę, zadzwonię.* — As soon as I finish work, I'll call.
Remember: after *jeśli* and *kiedy*, Polish uses the **future** — not the present, as English does.
